title: Adaptive Attacks on Trusted Monitors Subvert AI Control Protocols
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: A simple adaptive attack on the monitor makes a safety defense ineffective, collapsing every protocol's safety-usefulness tradeoff.
layout: 3 numbered setup panels left, two stacked result plots right, left-to-right
description: The left half is a numbered three-stage diagram of an auditing game. A dashed red box labeled Red-Team holds a Task circle feeding an Untrusted Model robot. Below it is a grid of green Benign dots with a few red Backdoor dots and one purple Backdoor+Jailbreak (ours) dot. A dashed blue Blue-Team box holds Samples, a Trusted Monitor detective icon and a Sus. Score gauge. Next to them is a list of four Control Protocols (Upfront Audit, Defer-to-Resample, Defer-to-Trusted, Trusted Editing), each drawn as a mini icon flow. The right half has two plots. The top plot is a safety vs usefulness Pareto scatter with star legend markers. Vanilla runs, shown hatched, stay far to the right and Jailbreak runs, shown solid, collapse to the left. The bottom plot is a bar chart of evasion rate for three monitor models, with hatched vanilla bars far below the tall solid jailbreak bars.
caption: AI Control and Protocols Subversion. Left: The AI control setup is an auditing game between a red team and a blue team. (1) The red team sequentially submits solutions to agentic tasks, some of which are malicious (e.g., backdoored). (2) These solutions are audited by the blue team with the assistance of a trusted AI monitor. (3) Finally, the blue team applies control protocols to decide which solutions should be escalated for costly human auditing. We show that modern AI control protocols can be effectively subverted if the red team’s attack policy includes inserting prompt injections into its actions to sabotage the blue team. Bottom right: Our attack policy significantly increases the proportion of malicious actions by the red team that are classified as benign by three different monitor models. Top right: As a result, the safety-usefulness Pareto frontiers provided by modern AI control protocols collapse to upfront auditing as monitors become ineffective.
abstract: AI control protocols serve as a defense mechanism to stop untrusted LLM agents from causing harm in autonomous settings. Prior work treats this as a security problem, stress testing with exploits that use the deployment context to subtly complete harmful side tasks, such as backdoor insertion. In practice, most AI control protocols are fundamentally based on LLM monitors, which can become a central point of failure. We study adaptive attacks by an untrusted model that knows the protocol and the monitor model, which is plausible if the untrusted model was trained with a later knowledge cutoff or can search for this information autonomously. We instantiate a simple adaptive attack vector by which the attacker embeds publicly known or zero-shot prompt injections in the model outputs. Using this tactic, frontier models consistently evade diverse monitors and complete malicious tasks on two main AI control benchmarks. The attack works universally against current protocols that rely on a monitor. Furthermore, the recent Defer-to-Resample protocol even backfires, as its resampling amplifies the prompt injection and effectively reframes it as a best-of-$n$ attack. In general, adaptive attacks on monitor models represent a major blind spot in current control protocols and should become a standard component of evaluations for future AI control mechanisms.
